Tantalum watch cases are a fascinating niche in the world of horology. Tantalum, a rare and dense metal, has increasingly become a choice material for luxury watchmakers seeking to differentiate their timepieces. Here’s why tantalum is gaining popularity in watchmaking: Durability : Tantalum is renowned for its exceptional durability and resistance to corrosion, making it an ideal material for watch cases. It can withstand the rigors of daily wear, scratches, and environmental factors, ensuring that the watch retains its luster and appearance over time. Unique Aesthetic : Tantalum’s distinctive dark grey hue sets it apart from traditional watch case materials like stainless steel or gold. Its deep, lustrous sheen adds an air of sophistication and exclusivity to the timepiece, appealing to collectors and connoisseurs who appreciate unique aesthetics. Hypoallergenic Properties : Tantalum is hypoallergenic, making it an excellent choice for individuals with sensitive skin or metal allergies. This property ensures that wearers can enjoy their timepiece comfortably without any adverse reactions. High Density : Tantalum is a dense metal, which gives tantalum watch cases a substantial feel on the wrist. This weightiness adds to the luxury feel of the timepiece and provides a sense of quality craftsmanship. Craftsmanship Challenges : Working with tantalum presents unique challenges due to its high melting point and resistance to corrosion. However, skilled watchmakers have developed techniques to overcome these obstacles, resulting in finely crafted tantalum watch cases that meet the highest standards of quality and precision. Limited Availability : Tantalum’s rarity adds to its allure in the world of luxury watches. Its limited availability contributes to the exclusivity of tantalum timepieces, making them highly coveted among collectors. Overall, tantalum watch cases offer a blend of durability, unique aesthetics, and exclusivity that appeal to discerning watch enthusiasts. As the demand for distinctive and high-quality timepieces continues to grow, tantalum is likely to remain a sought-after material in the realm of luxury watchmaking. At the heart of this creation lies an off-white Grand Feu enamel dial — a work of patience and precision that embodies the quiet perfection of true craftsmanship. Fired repeatedly at nearly 900°C, the dial achieves a serene, glass-like finish that will never fade with time. Each piece is individually hand-crafted, ensuring subtle variations that make every dial unique. The enamel’s soft, ivory tone reflects Singapore’s balance between heritage and modernity — understated yet luminous, sophisticated yet confident. Subtle red accents pay tribute to the nation’s vitality and strength, while the case, crafted entirely from polished tantalum, embodies HP Hercules’ pursuit of enduring substance.

watches.name: 7 Summits Edition
watches.description: We craft an exclusive series of timepieces for Seven Summits enthusiasts. Choose your preferred summit, and we’ll engrave its elevation profile directly onto the movement—illuminated with SuperLuminova for a striking touch. A personal engraving on the caseback completes the piece, making it a lasting tribute to your achievement and a meaningful heirloom for the next generation. Flexible payment plans are available— contact us to learn more. The Seven Summits The Seven Summits represent the highest mountains on each of the seven continents—a formidable mountaineering challenge that has captivated climbers worldwide. Completing the Seven Summits is considered one of the greatest achievements in the world of high-altitude exploration, demanding not only peak physical fitness and technical skill but also deep resilience and an indomitable spirit. The idea of the Seven Summits was first conceived by Richard Bass , an American businessman and mountaineer, who completed the challenge in 1985. Bass’s list included the highest peaks on each continent, but it was Reinhold Messner who completed his version in 1986, the legendary Italian alpinist and visionary, who proposed a variation that better reflected both geographical and mountaineering accuracy. Messner’s version replaced Mount Kosciuszko in Australia (a relatively modest climb) with Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid) in Papua, Indonesia—considered a much more technically challenging and geographically valid representation of the Australian continent’s highest peak. Thus was born the Messner version of the Seven Summits, which quickly gained respect among elite climbers for its authenticity and difficulty. We follow in this series the Messner version of the seven summits. 1. Mount Everest (Asia) Elevation: 8,848 meters (29,029 feet) Location: Nepal/Tibet (China) Range: Himalayas First Ascent: 1953 by Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay Notable Facts: Known as “Chomolungma” in Tibetan and “Sagarmatha” in Nepali, Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth. Climbers face extreme altitude, unpredictable weather, and the infamous “Death Zone” above 8,000 meters, where oxygen levels are critically low. 2. Aconcagua (South America) Elevation: 6,961 meters (22,838 feet) Location: Argentina Range: Andes First Ascent: 1897 by Matthias Zurbriggen Notable Facts: Aconcagua is the highest peak outside of Asia and the tallest in both the Western and Southern Hemispheres. While it doesn’t require technical climbing skills, the high altitude and severe weather conditions pose significant challenges. 3. Denali (North America) Elevation: 6,190 meters (20,310 feet) Location: Alaska, USA Range: Alaska Range First Ascent: 1913 by Hudson Stuck, Harry Karstens, Walter Harper, and Robert Tatum Notable Facts: Denali, formerly known as Mount McKinley, is renowned for its extreme cold, unpredictable weather, and significant elevation gain from base to summit. Its remote location and challenging conditions make it one of the most demanding climbs. 4. Kilimanjaro (Africa) Elevation: 5,895 meters (19,341 feet) Location: Tanzania Range: Free-standing volcanic massif First Ascent: 1889 by Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller Notable Facts: Kilimanjaro is the highest free-standing mountain in the world and offers climbers a journey through diverse ecosystems, from lush rainforests to arctic-like summit conditions. It’s considered the most accessible of the Seven Summits, requiring no technical climbing skills. 5. Mount Elbrus (Europe) Elevation: 5,642 meters (18,510 feet) Location: Russia Range: Caucasus Mountains First Ascent: 1874 by a British expedition Notable Facts: Elbrus is a dormant volcano with two summits, the western being the higher. While considered one of the more straightforward climbs among the Seven Summits, climbers must be prepared for glacier travel and rapidly changing weather conditions. 6. Mount Vinson (Antarctica) Elevation: 4,892

watches.name: Custom Dial Handpainted
watches.description: We are honoured to work on these projects with the talented Rachal Monard from RS Cadrans in Switzerland. She can paint anything you want on your custom watch dial—whether it’s mountains, people, animals, or anything else. Feel free to contact us for more details and pricing information. Flexible payment plans are available— contact us to learn more. Old German Advertisement Here you can see an old ad from Henzi & Pfaff advertising the watch that went up the mountain. If you look closely, you can see that the dial and hands are very strongly influenced by the original watch. Numeral indexes on the 3 – 6 – 9 and 12 hours, bright white dial, “sword” hands for the hour and minutes and finally a long central second hand. The second hand is colored in a dark blood red color, memorating the people who didn’t return from the Nanga Parbat. See history of Hercules ↗ The movement The movement is specially made for Hercules in collaboration with Manufacture horlogère Vallée de Joux in the middle of the Swiss Jura mountains. This hand wound movement is extra special due to two barrels bringing extra power to the geartrain. This makes it possible to keep running for 120 hours (5 days) when fully wound. The alpinism part comes from the height lines of the Nanga Parbat (like on an old map) engraved in the bridges, filled with BGW9 SuperLuminova. This lights up bright blue in the night, memorating the permafrost on the top of the mountain.

The second hand is colored in a dark blood red color, memorating the people who didn’t return from the Nanga Parbat. See history of Hercules ↗ The movement The movement is specially made from scratch for this watch. The luxury aspect comes mainly from the micro-rotor mechanism. Normally, an automatic rotor is placed on top of a movement, while here the rotor is placed between the bridges. The alpinism part comes from the height lines of the Nanga Parbat (like on an old map) engraved in the bridges, filled with BGW9 SuperLuminova. This lights up bright blue in the night, memorating the permafrost on the top of the mountain.
